approachQuestion.prompt:
Circular inspection

There are n stations in a directed circle, indexed 0..n-1. At station i you collect fuel[i], then spend cost[i] to reach the next station. Start with an empty tank of unlimited capacity. Return any station index from which a full circuit is possible, or -1 if none exists.

Example 1: fuel=[1,4,1], cost=[2,1,3] → 1. Starting at 1 leaves fuel 3, then 1, then 0.
Example 2: fuel=[0,1], cost=[2,0] → -1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; both arrays have length n; 0 ≤ fuel[i],cost[i] ≤ 10^9. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Scan differences fuel[i]-cost[i], maintaining total and a candidate tank. Whenever the candidate tank becomes negative, set the candidate start to i+1 and reset its tank to zero. Return -1 if total is negative; otherwise return the candidate start modulo n.
options.feedback: When a candidate first fails at i, every station between that start and i also fails: removing a nonnegative earlier prefix cannot repair the deficit. If total is nonnegative, the remaining candidate can complete the wrapped suffix and prefix.

options.text: Start at the station with the largest individual fuel amount; test only that start.
options.feedback: A large refill may have an even larger outgoing cost. With fuel=[5,4], cost=[6,1], station 0 fails but station 1 completes the circuit.

options.text: Return 0 whenever total fuel is at least total cost.
options.feedback: Total sufficiency guarantees some start, not start 0. With fuel=[0,2], cost=[1,1], only station 1 works.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: One scan updates a total and one candidate tank.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Every station contributes once to both total and candidate tank. Resetting a tank does not restart scanning, so worst-case work is O(n). Candidate start, two sums, and the index use O(1) auxiliary space.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
